name: Bilal Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of a primary teaching degree. My week is lectures on child development, maths and literacy, plus a school visit on Thursdays where I help in a Year 3 class. I live with my parents and two younger sisters in a small flat, and on Saturdays and Sundays I work at the hardware store on Fenner Road, mixing paint and carrying bags of cement. On Tuesday evenings I coach the under-nines at the local football club for free. I like being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a bit more software, a few jobs changed, but nothing wild. Teaching is about turning up for kids every day. I'd say good teachers will always be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd carry on as usual. My worry is that teaching pay is modest and my loan will be big. If prices go up, I'd be stretched. But I'd have a job, and that matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the hardware store and coaching, and I'd ask the school for a chance to help with after-school clubs. I'd use AI sometimes for lesson ideas, once my lecturers say it's fine. I'd save a little every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit tired, but good tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like being useful. What does that look like on a Saturday at the hardware store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone comes in with a leaking tap and no idea what they need, and I send them home with the right washer and a smile. They come back a week later to say thanks. I like that more than I like the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who is thinking about teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it if you like kids, because it's a calling as much as a job. The pay isn't huge but a school is a community, and you'd be part of it. I'd also say get some real classroom time early, to be sure.

say: I'd say it's what I expected: a bit more **software**, but nothing wild.
I'd say good **teachers** will always be needed.
think: Privately, I'd carry on as usual; my worry is **modest** pay and a big loan.
If prices rise I'd be **stretched**, but I'd have a job.
do: Keep the **hardware** store job and the football coaching.
Ask the school about helping with **after-school** clubs and save a little each month.
feel: **Settled**, mostly; a bit tired, but good tired.
S0.quote: Someone comes in with a leaking tap and no idea what they need, and I send them home with the right washer and a smile.
fieldNote: He takes pride in being **useful**, at the store and on the football pitch.
Money is a quiet pressure: a modest teacher's pay and a growing loan.

steps.text: Keep working weekends at the Fenner Road hardware store
Ask the school to help with after-school clubs
Save a little from every wage towards books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will handle some of the marking and planning, and the rest stays human. I'd tell the lads at the football club that they'll still need a teacher who knows their name. And I'd say it's about time schools got help with the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit wary. If AI does a lot of the preparation, schools might need fewer teachers or fewer teaching assistants. And I'm in a job where the first post matters. But I think a good teacher is still worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools my university shows us, since I'm usually okay once others have tried something. I'd ask the school how they use it and keep both jobs. I'd also volunteer for the extra things that need a real person, like trips and clubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy but fine. I'd say I'm cautious rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of teaching do you think software takes over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say work hard and the rest follows. My mum would worry about me taking on a loan for a job that might change. They'd both ask if I'm sure, and I'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think your parents would react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The teaching assistants. They're the ones schools can cut first, and they're the people kids often talk to. I'd stand up for them if I could.

say: I'd say software handles some **marking** and planning, but the rest stays human.
I'd say kids still need a teacher who knows their **name**.
think: Privately, I'd be **wary**: schools might need fewer teachers or assistants.
A good teacher is still worth **keeping**.
do: Learn the tools my **university** shows us, once others have tried them.
Volunteer for **trips** and clubs that need a real person.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, but cautious rather than scared.
S1.quote: The teaching assistants. They're the ones schools can cut first, and they're the people kids often talk to.
fieldNote: He expects the **assistants** to be cut first and wants to protect the human parts of school.
Steady in temperament, he learns tools after others have tested them.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools my university introduces
Volunteer for school trips and clubs that need a person
Ask the Year 3 teacher how the school uses software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless to rush something this big, and that families need protection. I'd say work and community have always carried us through. I'd say we need leaders who care about ordinary people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be rattled. I'd be partway through my degree when AI can do almost any thinking job, including the planning part of teaching. Robots for the hands-on side come three years later. My parents would need me to earn quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more at the store, save every pound and talk to my tutors about what a teacher looks like in 2030. I'd keep coaching, because it matters whatever happens. And I'd go to church and the community centre to hear what people are saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd try to look calm for my sisters, but I'd feel it in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after hearing it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sisters, Hana and Lila, that school is still important and they should learn how to talk to people and work hard. I'd tell my sisters to be kind, because that never goes out of date. They'd roll their eyes, but Hana would remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sisters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan. If AI cuts teaching jobs, I'd be paying for a degree with no post to go to. I'd need to move fast on something else, and I'd be doing that with no cushion.

say: I'd say it's **reckless** to rush something this big, and families need protection.
I'd say we need leaders who care about **ordinary** people.
think: Privately, I'd be **rattled**: AI could do the planning half of teaching before I finish.
My parents would need me to **earn** quickly.
do: Work more at the **store** and save every pound.
Talk to my **tutors** about what a teacher looks like in 2030, and keep coaching.
feel: **Anxious**; calm for my sisters, but tight in the chest.
S2.quote: I'd tell my sisters to be kind, because that never goes out of date.
fieldNote: He tries to protect his **sisters** from the fear and turns to community and work.
The loan with no **post** to go to is his sharpest worry.

steps.text: Work more weekend hours at the hardware store
Ask tutors what teaching will look like by 2030
Keep coaching the under-nines on Tuesdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning. Schools, parents and the government should talk about it now and make sensible plans. I'd say teachers should be included in the discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel okay. I'd qualify, teach for two years and see what happens before robots arrive. I'd be young enough to adjust, and teaching is the kind of job that keeps people around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a placement at a school that's trying new tools and keep both jobs for money. I'd learn what the tools can do once a few teachers I trust use them. I'd save a bit each month for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably steady. It's a challenge, but I'd know what I'm facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives more time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That schools use the tools as an excuse to save money. I'd want a teacher in every classroom, not a screen with a smiling face. I'd say so at a parents' evening or at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' jobs. My dad works in a warehouse, and my mum cleans at a school. The robots would reach them in time, and I'd want to be earning by then, so I could help.

say: I'd say five years is a fair **warning**, and teachers should be part of the discussion.
I'd say schools should make sensible **plans** now.
think: Privately, I'd feel **okay**: qualify, teach for two years and adjust.
Teaching is the kind of job that keeps people **around**.
do: Take a **placement** at a school trying new tools and keep both jobs.
Learn the tools once teachers I **trust** use them, and save monthly.
feel: Reasonably **steady**; a challenge, but I'd know what I'm facing.
S3.quote: I'd want a teacher in every classroom, not a screen with a smiling face.
fieldNote: His **faith** in the teaching profession keeps him steady in the five-year world.
He worries more about his **parents'** warehouse and cleaning jobs than about his own.

steps.text: Take a placement at a school trying new tools
Keep both weekend jobs while studying
Save a little each month for a rainy day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it's a chance to build things properly. I'd say communities should look after their young people and teach them to work with their hands and their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd qualify, teach for about seven years and maybe become a deputy head. I might even coach full time at a youth academy. The robots would come in when I'm already established.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a teaching post, and settle near my parents. I'd help my sisters through school and save for a small flat. I'd keep coaching on Tuesdays, because it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I'd get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a house with a garden and a few kids of my own someday. Ten years gives me time for that. I'd want them to grow up in a place where a teacher still knows their name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people stop talking to each other. If machines do the thinking and robots do the lifting, I'd worry about what's left for people to be proud of. I'd say work gives people dignity, and I'd hate to lose that.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, and communities should teach young people to work with hands and heads.
I'd say it's a chance to build things **properly**.
think: Privately, I'd feel **good**: qualify, teach for seven years and maybe become a deputy head.
Robots would come when I'm already **established**.
do: Finish the degree, get a teaching **post** and settle near my parents.
Help my sisters through school, save for a small **flat** and keep coaching.
feel: Pretty **calm**; I'd get on with life.
S4.quote: Work gives people dignity, and I'd hate to lose that.
fieldNote: The long runway lets him picture **family** life, a flat and a teaching career.
His remaining concern is about **dignity** and community, not about money or his own job.

steps.text: Finish the degree and take a teaching post near home
Keep coaching the under-nines every Tuesday

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd be mid-degree, with a loan, and my parents' jobs could be on the line too. What would help is honest notice from the government and some protection for the teaching jobs that need a real person. One thing you didn't ask: I keep thinking about the kids at my football club. For some of the kids at my football club, I'm the only adult who shows up every week.

portrait: Bilal is a **primary teaching** student who lives with his parents and two sisters and works weekends at a hardware store.
He coaches under-nines football for free and values being **useful** above pay.
Traditional and steady, he adopts new tools once others have tried them and trusts **work** and community.
His worry is the **loan** and his parents' warehouse and cleaning jobs, more than his own post.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries him most: mid-degree, with a loan, and his parents' jobs at risk too.
